title: Economics · Episode 1
chapters: Supply and demand: why things cost what they do
Externalities: the costs nobody pays for
Incentives: why rewards so often backfire

units.t: Economics. Episode one.
In this episode: Supply and demand: why things cost what they do, Externalities: the costs nobody pays for, Monopolies and why competition matters and Incentives: why rewards so often backfire.
Part one. Supply and demand: why things cost what they do.
Why avocados are cheap one month and pricey the next, why concert tickets vanish in minutes, and why rents keep rising.
Prices are signals.
Every price you see is a signal.
In a market economy, prices aren't set by a central planner; they emerge from millions of decisions by buyers and sellers.
A high price signals that something is scarce or much wanted, encouraging producers to make more and buyers to use less.
A low price signals the opposite.
Economist Friedrich Hayek argued this is one of the market's most remarkable features: prices coordinate the actions of millions of people who've never met and don't know why things changed.
Demand and supply.
Demand describes how much people want to buy at different prices.
Generally, the lower the price, the more they buy.
That's the law of demand.
Demand also shifts for other reasons: income, tastes, the price of alternatives, expectations and population.
When avocado toast became a café trend, demand for avocados rose at every price.
Supply describes how much sellers will produce at different prices.
Higher prices encourage more supply, because producing becomes more profitable.
Supply shifts with costs, technology, weather and the number of producers.
After Cyclone Larry wiped out Queensland banana crops in 2006, banana prices soared to around $12 or more a kilogram.
Where they meet.
Put supply and demand together and the price tends to settle where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.
Economists call this the equilibrium.
If the price is above it, sellers have unsold stock and cut prices.
If it's below it, buyers compete for too few goods and prices rise.
This constant push and pull explains everyday price changes: strawberries are cheap in peak season when supply floods in, and dear in the off-season when they're scarce.
Elasticity and price.
Some things you'll buy almost regardless of price, at least in the short term, like petrol to get to work, electricity or essential medicines.
Demand for these is called inelastic.
Other things you can easily skip or swap, like a particular brand of chips or a restaurant meal, so demand is elastic: a price rise sends buyers elsewhere.
Elasticity explains why governments tax items like tobacco and fuel, which people keep buying, and why businesses fight so hard over competitive products.
When prices can't adjust.
In March 2020, Australians rushed to buy toilet paper.
Demand spiked while supply couldn't adjust overnight, and supermarkets kept prices steady and set purchase limits instead.
Production never ran short; fear drove the surge, and shelves refilled within weeks.
Tickets for a hugely popular artist are often priced below what fans will pay, so they sell out in minutes and scalpers resell them higher.
Some sellers now use dynamic pricing, raising prices with demand.
Several Australian states cap ticket resale prices.
Housing is a supply story.
If new homes don't keep pace with population growth, because of land, planning rules, costs or labour shortages, prices and rents climb.
Low vacancy rates give landlords more pricing power.
The key idea: In a market, prices carry information about scarcity and desire, coordinating millions of people without a central planner.
Part two. Externalities: the costs nobody pays for.
When a factory pollutes a river, someone pays the price, just not the factory or its customers.
That gap is one of the biggest ideas in economics.
The leaf blower.
It's 7am on Sunday, and your neighbour fires up a petrol leaf blower.
They get a tidy driveway.
You get a ruined sleep in.
Your lost rest doesn't appear on their bill, so it doesn't factor into their decision.
Economists call this an externality: a side effect of an activity that falls on people outside the transaction.
Externalities can be negative, like noise, pollution or congestion, or positive, like a neighbour's beautiful garden.
Markets match prices to costs and benefits.
When some sit outside the price, markets can produce too much of the harmful stuff and too little of the helpful, often called a market failure.
Pigou and Coase.
In his 1920 book The Economics of Welfare, Arthur Pigou noted that the private cost of an activity can differ from its social cost, which includes harm to others.
A factory owner pays for fuel and wages, not for the coughing downwind.
His solution: tax the harm by the damage it causes, so the price reflects the true cost.
Such charges are called Pigouvian taxes, and economists across much of the political spectrum like them.
In 1960 Ronald Coase argued taxes aren't always the answer.
If rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the parties might negotiate: neighbours pay for filters, or the factory compensates them.
The catch, as Coase stressed, is that bargaining is often costly.
You can't negotiate with millions affected by air pollution, so governments usually step in.
Positive spillovers.
Externalities aren't all bad news.
When you get vaccinated, you lower your own risk but also make it harder for disease to spread to others, including people who can't be vaccinated.
Education ripples out to employers, colleagues and the wider community.
A beekeeper's bees pollinate nearby orchards without sending the orchardist a bill.
The problem is the mirror image of the negative kind: because people don't capture all the benefits, they may do less of the good thing than society would like.
That's one reason governments subsidise or provide things such as vaccination programs, schooling and research.
Debate continues about exactly how much support is justified, but the economic logic is widely accepted.
The commons.
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the 'tragedy of the commons'.
Imagine a pasture open to all herders.
Each gains from adding another cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture ends up ruined.
Overfishing is a classic example: each boat has an incentive to catch more before others do.
Hardin thought the only solutions were government control or private ownership.
Elinor Ostrom disagreed.
She studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems around the world and found that many communities manage shared resources successfully with their own local rules, monitoring and penalties.
In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Oliver Williamson.
Pricing harm.
Pigou's idea shows up in daily life.
London introduced a congestion charge in 2003, and Stockholm and Singapore have similar schemes.
Container deposit schemes, now in every Australian state and territory, put a small refundable value on bottles and cans.
Carbon pricing charges for emissions through a tax or a cap and trade system where companies trade permits.
Australia had a carbon price from 2012 until 2014, and the topic remains politically contested.
Externalities are everywhere: each extra car slows everyone on a busy road, and a loud phone call costs train passengers their peace.
Many are handled by manners and norms.
A useful question: who gets the benefit, who bears the cost, and do they line up?
When they don't, trouble usually follows.
The key idea: An externality is a cost or benefit that lands on people outside the transaction, so the price misses it.
Part three. Monopolies and why competition matters.
The board game Monopoly was invented to warn people about monopolies.
More than a century later, governments are still wrestling with the same problem.
A game about greed.
In 1904 Lizzie Magie patented The Landlord's Game, built to show how concentrated land ownership makes a few people rich and bankrupts the rest.
Players bought property and charged rent until one had crushed the others.
Versions spread informally before Parker Brothers sold Monopoly in the 1930s, and Charles Darrow was long credited as its sole inventor.
The irony is striking: a warning against monopolies became a celebration of them.
Strictly, a monopoly is a market with a single seller.
In practice, regulators worry about any firm with enough market power to raise prices or cut quality without losing customers.
Competition works the opposite way: if one cafe overcharges, you walk to the next.
Markets with two or three big players, called duopolies and oligopolies, may compete fiercely or settle into a comfortable pattern.
Rockefeller's oil empire.
In the late 1800s John D.
Rockefeller built Standard Oil into one of the most powerful companies in history.
It grew partly through genuine efficiency, cutting the cost of refining kerosene for lamps.
But it also used aggressive tactics, including secret deals with railways for cheaper transport and pushing rivals to sell or face ruin.
At its height Standard Oil controlled the great majority of oil refining in the United States.
Public anger led to new antitrust laws, and in 1911 the US Supreme Court ordered the company broken up into dozens of separate firms.
Some of those pieces grew into giants of their own, and later became part of companies like ExxonMobil and Chevron.
Natural monopolies.
Not every monopoly is a villain.
In a natural monopoly, competing networks make no sense.
Imagine three companies each laying their own water pipes down your street, or building separate sets of electricity poles.
The cost would be enormous and pointless.
In these cases one network is usually allowed to operate, but its prices and service are regulated, or it is owned by the government.
In Australia, independent regulators oversee the poles and wires that carry electricity and limit what network owners can charge.
Retailers then compete to sell electricity across those shared networks.
The goal is to keep the efficiency of a single network while protecting customers from monopoly prices.
Australia's competition watchdog.
Australian competition law is mainly set out in the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and enforced by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, the ACCC.
It is illegal for competitors to form a cartel, secretly agreeing to fix prices, share out customers or rig bids, and serious cartel conduct can be a criminal offence.
Companies with substantial market power are also banned from using it in ways that substantially lessen competition.
Since 2026, larger mergers must be notified to the ACCC and cannot go ahead without its approval, so it can block a deal that would leave customers with too little choice.
Australia's relatively small population means many markets have only a few big players, from supermarkets to airlines, so these questions come up often in public debate.
Digital age, daily life.
Older competition laws were built around prices: if a monopoly charged too much, that was the harm.
But many of today's most powerful companies offer products that are free, such as search and social media.
They earn money from advertising and data, which makes their power harder to measure.
Network effects mean the biggest platforms keep growing.
In 2024 a United States court ruled that Google had illegally maintained a monopoly in online search, and the European Union has placed special obligations on the largest digital gatekeepers.
Competition touches daily life.
When airlines compete on a route, fares tend to fall, and firms that stop improving lose customers to those that do.
Shopping around and switching providers keeps markets healthy.
The ACCC website explains how to report suspected collusion.
The key idea: Monopoly began as a warning, and a monopoly means one seller facing little real competition.
Part four. Incentives: why rewards so often backfire.
Offer people a reward and they'll respond, just not always the way you hoped.
Here's why clever incentives can go spectacularly wrong.
The great rat hunt.
In 1902 French colonial authorities in Hanoi faced rats in the city's new sewers, and plague made it urgent.
They offered a small bounty for every rat killed, paid on presentation of a tail.
Soon officials noticed rats running around without tails.
People were cutting off tails for the reward and releasing the rats to breed.
The historian Michael Vann found reports of rat farming too.
The scheme did what it paid for, not what it meant.
People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer intended.
It's one of the most important and most forgotten lessons in economics.
People respond.
If there's one sentence many economists would put on a T shirt, it's 'people respond to incentives'.
An incentive is anything that makes an action more or less attractive: a price, a bonus, a fine, a deadline, even praise or embarrassment.
Raise the price of something and people tend to buy less of it.
Many responses are what policymakers want.
Australia's container deposit schemes and rooftop solar incentives have changed behaviour on a large scale.
The trouble comes when incentives are designed carelessly, because people are quick to find the easiest path to a reward, whether or not it achieves the actual goal.
Measures as targets.
In 1975 the economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistics used to guide policy tend to break down once they become targets.
Marilyn Strathern later summed it up: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.'
A call centre rewarding short call times may find staff hanging up on difficult customers.
A hospital judged on waiting times may find creative ways to reclassify waits.
Schools judged on test scores can end up teaching to the test.
There's an old Soviet era joke about a nail factory: given a target by weight, it made a few giant useless nails; given a target by number, it made millions of tiny ones.
Whatever gets measured gets gamed.
Fines and crowding out.
In a 2000 study, Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini looked at Israeli day care centres where parents were often late.
Some introduced a small fine, and lateness rose.
The paper's title, 'A Fine Is a Price', gives the reason: late pick-up had meant imposing on a teacher's goodwill, but now it felt like a service parents could buy.
When the fines were removed, lateness stayed high.
A cheap financial incentive had replaced a social one, and the old norm didn't return.
Money can crowd out other motives.
In 1970 Richard Titmuss argued that paying for blood could undermine the civic duty of voluntary donors.
Researchers debate how strong this is, and payment raises effort in many settings.
But people are also motivated by pride, fairness and belonging.
Australia's Lifeblood relies on unpaid volunteers.
Moral hazard and design.
Moral hazard is an insurance term: if someone else bears the cost when things go wrong, people may be less careful.
A driver with comprehensive insurance might park carelessly.
A bank expecting a rescue might make riskier loans, keeping profits and passing losses to taxpayers, a worry after 2008.
Insurers use excesses so customers share part of every claim.
It can be managed, not eliminated.
Australia's banking Royal Commission, which reported in 2019, heard many examples of staff chasing commissions and sales targets at customers' expense.
To design better incentives, reward the true goal rather than an easy proxy, imagine how a cynical person might game it and close those loopholes, and use several measures.
Pride, trust and fairness are incentives too.
Ask the rat tail question: what am I really paying for?
The key idea: People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer meant.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does a high price usually signal in a market?
Answer. That something is scarce or much wanted.
Question two. Why does the leaf blower example show an externality?
Answer. The noise costs you, not the person making it.
Question three. What was the original purpose of Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game?
Answer. To show how land monopoly enriches only a few.
Question four. What went wrong with the Hanoi rat bounty?
Answer. People bred rats and cut off tails for cash.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
